segments.text: You know what feels absolutely
incredible to use from a front-end point
of view when you're working with agents,
reducers, and state machines. A reducer
kind of looks like this. It's got some
persistent state, and then it has a
bunch of actions. So, here we've got
open the camera, and then close the
camera, and then photo captured, etc.
All of these actions are things that can
happen based on the front-end UI. So,
these are events that could trigger
based on user actions or things failing,
etc. And then all the reducer does is it
takes in those actions and returns a new
state. So, on a very basic level, you've
got open camera, which returns open
camera true, and then close camera,
which returns open camera open false.
Now, this does something very, very
important, which is it separates the
user interface from the logic that
controls that user interface. That means
that this function, this thumbnail state
reducer, what it can do, it can be
tested independently outside of the
browser. So, the tests for it are very,
very fast. And we can see, for instance,
in the thumbnails page where we have a
button on click dispatch open camera, it
means that the actual user interface is
very stupid. The React code is very
dumb. In other words, we're
concentrating a lot of the logic for the
front-end code in a single place that's
easy to test, easy to modify, and easy
to see the entire thing of how it all
works together. And so, I can actually
feel the difference when I work with a
page that has a reducer in it that an
agent has edited. The whole thing just
feels so much more robust, and it feels
like most of the edge cases are handled.
So, I'm actually going back over old
projects that I'm working on and
cranking up the number of reducers.
